13434-regeneration-being-an-account-of-t:
H. Rider Haggard, in 1910, reports the social work of the Salvation Army in Great Britain, dedicating the book to its officers and soldiers for self-sacrificing aid to the poor and wretched. He visits men's work in London, the Spa Road elevator, Great Peter Street shelter, free breakfast service, workshops at Hanbury Street, and the central labour bureau.

Women's work, emigration, and investigation departments complete the survey. Army workers say that if a girl cannot be managed by love, her case is beyond them, though that very seldom happens, and most cures hold. Haggard urges novelists to study shelters, where one shelter holds material for ten lifetimes. The book admires practical rescue work without preaching at its subjects.
22489-power-of-mental-imagery-being-the-:
Power of Mental Imagery is the fifth volume in a twelve-volume efficiency course. It builds directly on the preceding volume, The Trained Memory. That volume taught that memory works through four elements working together.

The four elements are Retention, Recall, Recognition, and Imagination. Two of them, Retention and Recall, were explained in that earlier book. This fifth volume takes up imagination's share in the process. Mental imagery, it argues, can be trained like a muscle. Readers were promised greater efficiency in business and study. The course belonged to the era's faith in mental training systems. It preserves mail-order self-improvement in its most confident form.
45115-appletons-popular-science-monthly-:
Appleton Popular Science Monthly for June eighteen ninety nine opens volume fifty five. William Jay Youmans edited the monthly his father Edward founded years before. Appleton of New York issued the volume covering May to October eighteen ninety nine. A portrait of Thomas Egleston fronts the June number in this copy.

The lead paper gives a new method to gauge the age of Niagara Falls. Frederick Wright drew his data from railroad work along the gorge face. Lyell and James Hall had visited the falls in eighteen forty one together. They lacked means to fix the rate the falls cut back upstream. Wright new figures stand apart from all estimates current before his.
45938-appletons-popular-science-monthly-:
Appletons' Popular Science Monthly was the leading American journal of science for the general reader. This file holds its August 1899 number, part of volume fifty-five, edited by William Jay Youmans. A portrait of Herbert Spencer, the philosopher the magazine championed, stands in the volume.

The lead essay, by the Columbia sociologist Franklin Giddings, takes up public charity and private vigilance. Giddings thanks the New York comptroller for indicting the abuse of public money given to private charities, three million dollars a year raised by tax with no public control. Other articles cover the science of the day. The number shows the monthly at work as a forum for a young science of society.
47708-biography-and-family-record-of-lor:
Biography and Family Record of Lorenzo Snow is a life by his sister Eliza. Snow held rank as one of the twelve chiefs of the Latter Day Saints. His sister wrote the life as a gift of love and as a kin vault. The book came out at Salt Lake City in the year eighteen eighty four.

Her front note says the book should pass hand to hand down the line. Kin yet unborn should trace their faith roots in its full tale. Words of the church founder head the page as a rule of life. Youth, call, toil, and faith trials fill the record in plain form. The work stands as a house relic as much as a life in print.
56599-the-fortunes-of-the-colville-famil:
Frank Smedley, the English novelist behind Frank Fairlegh and Lewis Arundel, wrote this domestic novel of the Colville family. George Routledge and Sons issued it in London. The subtitle promises a cloud with its silver lining. The opening chapter, called The Two Pictures, sets a rectory household at Ashburn against the shadow of loss at Christmas.

The first pages linger on the family group in the breakfast parlour. A grave father has silver threading his dark hair, and a small merry son of nine sits on his knee. The mother's face records a loving life, and a daughter of about eighteen completes the group. Smedley's manner is warm and digressive, with direct addresses to the reader about grief and affection. The novel belongs to the mid Victorian school of family fiction, where fortunes rise and fall inside the home.
regeneration-being-an-account-of-the-soc:
H. Rider Haggard wrote this account of the Salvation Army's social work in Great Britain in 1910, and dedicated it to the Army's officers and soldiers. He praises their self-sacrificing work for the poor and wretched throughout the world. A portrait of General Booth fronts the book.

The contents map men's social work in London: the Spa Road elevator, the Great Peter Street shelter, and a free breakfast service. Work with ex-criminals, a men's workshop in Hanbury Street, Whitechapel, and Sturge House on Bow Road follow. A central labour bureau and an international investigation department close the list, showing aid joined with training and jobs.
